summary: The article provides a largely accurate overview of RNOR status and its tax implications for returning NRIs, aligning well with the Income Tax Act, 1961.

claims.claim: Your tax liability in India largely depends on your residential status as defined by the Income Tax Act, 1961.
claims.note: Residential status under Section 6 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, determines tax liability.

claims.claim: You are considered an NRI if you are in India for less than 182 days in the relevant financial year.
claims.note: An individual is considered an NRI if they do not meet the conditions for being a resident, which primarily includes staying in India for less than 182 days in the financial year.

claims.claim: An individual becomes an ROR if they meet both of the following conditions: 1. They have been a resident in India for at least 2 out of the 10 financial years immediately preceding the relevant financial year. 2. They have been in India for a period of 730 days or more during the 7 financial years immediately preceding the relevant financial year.
claims.note: These are the correct additional conditions for an individual to be classified as Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) under the Income Tax Act, 1961.

claims.claim: You are considered an RNOR if you qualify as a 'Resident' based on your physical presence in India for the current financial year, but do not meet both conditions to be an 'Ordinarily Resident'. Specifically, you are an RNOR if you meet one of the following criteria: 1. You have been a Non-Resident in India for 9 out of the 10 financial years immediately preceding the relevant financial year. 2. You have been in India for a period of 729 days or less during the 7 financial years immediately preceding the relevant financial year.
claims.note: These are the correct conditions for an individual to be classified as Resident Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) under the Income Tax Act, 1961.

claims.claim: For an RNOR, income accruing or arising outside India is generally not taxable in India, unless it is derived from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India.
claims.note: Foreign-sourced income for an RNOR is generally tax-free in India, unless it is derived from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India.

claims.claim: Yes, funds from NRE accounts are fully repatriable. The principal and interest earned on NRE accounts are tax-exempt in India for all residential statuses, including RNOR and ROR.
claims.note: While NRE account principal is repatriable and tax-exempt for NRIs, the interest earned on NRE accounts becomes taxable once an individual becomes a resident for FEMA purposes, which typically happens upon returning to India with no intention of moving out, irrespective of their RNOR status.

article_title: RNOR Status: Saving Tax on Foreign Income for Returning NRIs
